sections.content_markdown: When the temperature of the ice reaches $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ absorbing the heat, they melt into liquid. The temperature remains stagnant at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ until all the ice cubes melt into the water. That proves $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ as the melting point of ice. The straight line in the temperature is called the melting point line. In the fig 2.09, line AB is the melting point line. Both ice and water exist through the length of the line. If we apply more heat, the temperature of water starts to rise. When it reaches $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, you'll see more heat will not be able to raise the temperature of water anymore. Rather, the water transforms into vapor. All the water will vaporize at this $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ temperature. If we apply more heat after that, the temperature of the water vapor will increase. The boiling point of water is $100^{\circ}\text{C}$. CD is the line of boiling point. Water and vapor co-exist at this line.

figures.caption: Fig 2.09: Graph of applying heat on ice.
figures.description: Line graph showing the temperature of ice/water/vapor plotted against time (heat absorbed) with labeled melting point line (AB) and boiling point line (CD).
